Paul Ryan concerned that automation is replacing human workers -- but there's a catch: At one Wisconsin dairy, U.S.-made robots are replacing cheap foreign workers

People don't get it. The changes that are coming down the pike are massive. We're not talking about having some jobs go away, we're talking about swaths of entire professions vanish. And I would prefer robots to swarms of 3rd world garbage.

Forever Peace by Joe Haldeman describes a world where we are almost there- rich nations people barely have to work because automation does everything for them and makes anythingb they want. Downside is government control.

Government control in a country where people don't have to spend every waking moment working just to make ends meet is different than in one where they do. Aside from our broken first past the post system, there's a general selection bias in politics. Why aren't you running for office? There are probably a lot of reasons, but a big one in general is that you don't have the time for it. In a world where working 40+ hours a week just to be able to work 40+ hours next week is no longer necessary, it would open the door for greater citizen involvement in government. Imagine a congress that wasn't mostly made up of old millionaires. The people in the government we call "representatives" might actually start becoming representative of the people themselves.
Yeah sure like humans will still be allowed to make decisions.

These things are all happening far faster than most people realize. Self driving vehicles for instance are going to destroy millions of jobs by themselves. Taxis, commercial transport, logistics, and just about everything is out the window in relatively short order. That's just scratching the surface of where we're headed but it's going to be a deep enough scratch that I think it will probably be the event that triggers mainstream discussion of transition towards a new socioeconomic standard. If everything goes at the pace most companies are targeting, we'd see this taking shape before our next president's first term is over.

In other words, this isn't some vague allusion to some far distant future where we can just hand-wave anything into (or out of) existence. This is happening now. Yes, humans will still be allowed to make decisions and we'll still be a democracy.

I don't think fully autonomous vehicles (no operator controls) will be ubiquitous in that short of timeframe but I guess we will see. I'd like to see more videos of these things driving around in traffic in really shitty weather under the worse case conditions that people drive in every day.

Let's go back to 2010. Self driving cars were being mentioned here and there but there wasn't any real action. Google's very small scale self driving car tests (with a professional at the wheel) wouldn't hit the roads until 2011-2012. Cutting edge was a handful of vehicle manufacturers that had created some vehicles that could parallel park themselves. How likely would you been to believe that by 2015 a company would have released and enabled public testing of a vehicle capable of complete autonomous driving on open roads? And that by 2016 those seem vehicles would have had more than 220 million road miles in autonomous mode?

The crazy thing about technology right now is that it doesn't seem to be advancing particularly fast on a day by day basis, but if you actually look at the state of things not that long ago - it feels like the stone age. Tesla's goal for full autonomy, as in your car is in New York and you tell it to come pick you up in LA and it works its way there, is 2018. Uber and Lyft are actively testing self driving taxis as well which means they probably see a similar timeline. The entire next presidency gives them a pretty healthy buffer for delays. And once that technology is developed to a release level by anybody anywhere, the transition to it will likely be incredibly swift.

AFAIK nobody is testing self driving taxis or any other vehicle without a driver onboard. Two hundred and twenty million miles sounds like a lot unless you consider that three trillion miles are driven annually in the US. Like I said I would be interested to see any videos of these vehicles operating in traffic in crappy weather especially torrential rain, heavy snow, or black ice. I am skeptical about the timetables being tossed around both in regard to fully autonomous vehicles that operate in all weather and manned flight to Mars.

If these things happen on schedule great.
But, you see, the real problem is robots don't vote.

It doesn't matter whether it's cheap foreign workers or expensive citizens that you're replacing, if they're all doing unskilled labour they're all going to be unemployed soon.

To put it in context, unemployment during the Great Depression was ~25%. About 25% of current jobs could be automated right now and it's just a matter of us getting around to it. In five years' time that number becomes more like 50-75%.

Our entire Western economic model needs a serious overhaul if we want to still be a functioning society in 2050.

Never underestimate the cost of having AI and robots to replace humans. Not the first years but as they age and break down, it is going to be more expensive than if you used a human. And what is worse you have lost the very people that could fix the issues since you outsourced them.
I think you are highly underestimating how cheap and how extensive automation (including self-repair or automated repair) will be.

Assuming repairing and maintaining robots is something only a human can do is, I think, rather missing the point. The really cool thing is that robotics/AI and also things like 3d printing technology are all evolving extremely rapidly in unison. The possibilities there are really only limited by one's imagination.
